senses: A person who installs shingles.
A metalworker who hammers and squeezes material to expel impurities.
A person who practices homeopathy.
ety: From homeo- + -path, related to German Homöopath.

senses: The female genitalia; the vulva or vagina.
examples: What everybody doesn't know is the hot pulsating goodies Helen Reddy's got to offer up. Cum here woman, do your duty; drop them drawers and gimme some pooty!

senses: Any set of four different pitch classes.
A series of four sounds, forming a scale of two-and-a-half tones.
Radiotherapy using radioactive sources positioned within (or close to) the treatment volume, typically with radiopharmaceuticals as opposed to external-beam sources.
ety: From Ancient Greek βραχύς (brakhús, “short, not far off”) + θεραπεία (therapeía, “attendance, treatment, healing, service”); brachy- + therapy.

senses: To decorate with sprigs, or with representations of sprigs, as in embroidery or pottery.
To nail the sole onto a shoe.
ety: From Middle English sprig, sprigge, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Middle Low German sprik, spricke (“a dry, easily broken twig that has fallen from a tree; sprig”). Compare also dialectal English sprag (“sprig, twig”), English spray (“branch”), Old English spræc (“a shoot”), German Low German Spricke, Sprick (“dry branch, twig”).

senses: An interpreter, especially for the Arabic and Turkish languages.
ety: From Middle English dragman, from Old French drugeman, from Medieval Latin dragumannus, from Byzantine Greek δραγομάνος (dragomános), from Arabic تُرْجُمَان (turjumān), from Classical Syriac ܬܰܪܓܡܳܢܳܐ (targmānā), from Akkadian 𒅴𒁄 (targumannum, “interpreter”). With the plural form -men, through reinterpretation as suffixed with -man. Doublet of truchman.
examples: Engaging William Prime's (q.v.) dragoman, he visits the bazaars, mosques, and Pyramids before sailing in the dahabeeya Rip Van Winkle up the Nile.

senses: To undo by removing a tether.
A tool that is used to trim the edges of a lawn.
A woodworking tool for straightening the edges of wood and cutting it into boards.
One who practises the sexual technique of edging.
An Iraqi-Jewish eggplant sandwich popular in Israel.
Of a liquid: thick; viscous.
Of a surface: sloppy, slimy.
Rainy, wet. (of weather)
A derisive or mocking expression of scorn, contempt, or reproach.
An object of scorn, mockery, or derision.
ety: From Middle English scof, skof, probably of North Germanic origin. Compare Old Norse skaup, Old Danish skof, Old Frisian skof (“insult, shame”), and Old High German scoph.

senses: To load down something with a burden.
To restrict or block something with a hindrance or impediment.
To burden with a legal claim or other obligation.
ety: From Middle English encombren, from Old French encombrer, from en- + combrer (“to hinder”) (See cumber). By surface analysis, en- + cumber.

senses: A person who makes or sells bows (for use with arrows).
ety: From Middle English bowyere, bowȝere, variant forms of bowere (“bowyer”), equivalent to bow + -yer.

senses: A service for sending, receiving, and/or storing email, usually on a remote web server, in such a way that it is accessible through a web browser.
The email thus stored.
examples: Hotmail, Yahoo! Mail and Gmail are well-known webmail services.
I'm going to check my webmail.

senses: Able to be flown; airworthy.
Passable by flight.
A man who operates a winch.
A ravine or gorge, usually one with water running through.
ety: From Middle English flum, from Old French flum, flun, from Latin flumen, from fluere (“to flow”).

senses: Synonym of uncertainty.
The physical substances which create the natural world: matter, materials, substance, etc.
ety: Borrowed from Latin māteria (“matter, the material world”).

senses: An altarpiece, especially one of multiple connected pictures
To remove the polarization from something.
To demagnetize.
A television set.

A (later partly) mechanical such apparatus, largely superseded during the 1930s by wholly electronic ones; originally and especially, one designed and patented by the Scottish inventor John Logie Baird (1888–1936).
An organization that makes or broadcasts television programs.
ety: Probably partly from televis(ion) + -or, and partly (in senses 2 and 3) from televise + -or. Appears to have been coined by the Scottish inventor John Logie Baird (1888–1936) in 1926 or earlier. A genericized trademark.
examples: Maybe, I am not yet mad but somewhat hypersensitive. So I prefer to make use of a TFT display and threw my televisor away in order to avoid getting red eyes.
A man stands up and switches on a televisor and everybody listens.
As for the BBC, they are officially the worst televisors of rugby I've yet seen.

senses: The moriche palm.
A groove or slot, often cut in a masonry wall or other vertical surface, for inserting an inset flashing component such as a reglet.
A ragged piece.
A person who excavates.
A vehicle, often on tracks, used to dig ditches etc.
A curette used to scrape out pathological material.
The act of making things parallel.
The act of making operations work in parallel, particularly in, but not limited to, computing.
Someone who exaggerates.
An agent of gentrification.
examples: This real-estate drama, however, has a twist: one of the area's gentrifiers is a stylish new restaurant and performance space opened by Michael Dorf, the founder of the Knitting Factory.

senses: To demobilize; to release someone from military service.
Bearing a cross.
ety: From Late Latin crucifer (“cross-bearing”) + -ous. By surface analysis, crucifer + -ous.

senses: A person who compiles bibliographies, or who studies bibliography.
An instance or act of undulating.
A wavy appearance or outline; waviness.
A tremulous tone produced by a peculiar pressure of the finger on a string.
A wavelike curve; a smooth and regular rise and fall.
A wavelike motion of the air; electromagnetic radiation.
ety: From undulate + -ion, or borrowed from Medieval Latin undulātiō; compare French ondulation.
examples: But the next undulation would raise us, showing the island ablaze in the sunlight, an emerald of dazzling beauty resting lightly on the bosom of the sea.

senses: Resembling a picturesque toy model.
Insignificant.
A percussion instrument that makes a clacking noise.
Any device that makes a clacking noise.
Multivalent; having a number of different forms, purposes, meanings, aspects or principles.
One who catches and returns a ball, usually out of play; one who fetches played balls; one who fetches shot game.
One who dances the shag; a jazz dancer.
examples: The shagger is placed in this position to avoid the danger of his being hit by a batted ball.
He always had a shagger, a caddy who put the shag bag right in front of his feet.

senses: A tendency among some conservative Christians, especially in the USA, to seek influence or control over secular civil government through political action.
The belief that human beings should be free to dominate and exploit nature, including plants and animals.
To render an object linear.
To treat in a linear manner.

A type of flat-bottomed freighter used on the Nile in Ancient Egypt, powered either by sail, or by being towed by a downstream raft driven by the current, while dragging a stone anchor to keep the course steady.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris), from Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare), from Demotic Egyptian br, from Egyptian bꜣjr b-bA-A-y:r*Z1-P1 Doublet of barge, bark and barque.
